title: AOM-based ultra-low noise laser intensity control up to the MHz range
authors: Christian Partes, Jonas Auch, Eduard Heidt, Kirill Karpov, Florian Kiesel, Christian Groß
abstract: High-power laser sources that exhibit low relative intensity noise and allow simultaneous dynamic control of their light level are required for a broad range of applications in various fields of physics. Acousto-optic modulators (AOMs) are widely used for active power stabilization and regulation due to their simple drive electronics requirements and high optical power handling capability in free-space. However, the rather slow propagation speed of the sound wave within the AOM crystal typically limits their control bandwidth to a few hundred kHz. In this work, we present a novel AOM-based control system that is capable of significantly suppressing intensity noise of high-power lasers up to the MHz range. By combining two standard feedback loops with one feedforward control branch and optimizing the beam path in the AOM crystal, ultra-low relative intensity noise levels down to $-155\, \text{dB}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}$ even at several hundred kHz are achieved. Our results are relevant for applications that require ultra-low intensity noise at Fourier frequencies up to the MHz range, such as optical lattice experiments with light ultracold atoms.
summary: The paper presents an advanced experimental technique to achieve ultra-low relative intensity noise in high-power lasers using Acousto-Optic Modulators (AOMs). By integrating a sophisticated control scheme involving both feedback and feedforward paths, the system stabilizes laser intensity up to the MHz range. This capability is crucial for next-generation quantum experiments involving light ultracold atoms.
main_problem: The development of high-power laser sources that maintain ultra-low relative intensity noise (RIN) while allowing dynamic control up to the MHz frequency range.
main_result: The authors achieved an ultra-low relative intensity noise level down to $-155 	ext{ dB Hz}^{-1}$ even at several hundred kHz by implementing a combined feedback and feedforward control system on an AOM platform.
method: A novel control architecture combining two standard feedback loops with one feedforward branch, implemented using photodiodes for measurement and FPGA/analog electronics for signal processing.
model_or_system: The experiment uses Acousto-Optic Modulators (AOMs) driven by RF mixers. The system incorporates a slow DC control loop for low-frequency stabilization and a fast AC loop, alongside feedforward compensation to suppress noise across a wide bandwidth.
key_observables: Relative Intensity Noise (RIN) spectrum, measured down to $-158 	ext{ dB Hz}^{-1}$ at the electronic limit; closed-loop bandwidth up to $1.2 	ext{ MHz}$.
important_parameters: Noise suppression of $>30 	ext{ dB}$; control bandwidth extending into the $	ext{MHz}$ range; AOM reaction times down to $65 	ext{ ns}$.
main_assumptions: The system relies on linearizing the non-linear AOM response using Gain-Scheduling and Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) algorithms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, detailing beam paths for DC and AC control branches. Other figures compare RIN spectra across different control regimes (free-running vs. fully controlled).
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of low-noise lasers, describes the physical AOM system, outlines the advanced signal processing combining feedback/feedforward loops, presents measurements showing noise suppression at high frequencies, and concludes with performance metrics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical technical requirement for modern AMO experiments, such as optical lattice physics, where laser intensity stability is paramount for trapping and manipulating ultracold atoms.
